declared.title: Lost in the mall again: a preregistered replication and extension of Loftus & Pickrell (1995)
declared.foundIn: OpenAlex search « Lost in the mall again: a preregistered replication and extension of Loftus and Pickrell » (2026-11-23)

population: 123 adults in Ireland (18-57, recruited through students' networks), interviewed twice about true childhood events and one made up from a relative's information

findings.text: A preregistered replication coded 35% of people as reporting a false memory of getting lost in a mall as a child (25% in the original study)

support.sentence: We replicated the findings of the original study, coding 35% of participants as reporting a false memory for getting lost in a mall in childhood (compared to 25% in the original study).

findings.text: Most of these were partial memories (27%); only 8% were full memories of the made-up event

support.sentence: Though the breakdown of full vs. partial memories was not included in the original paper, most of the false memories reported at the end of the current study were partial memories (27%) and a smaller portion were full memories (8%).
support.readBy: memory-rewritten reviser, 2026-11-26: accepted version, PsyArXiv nh3zq, Discussion

findings.text: The coded rate rose with each round of suggestion: 15% after the written booklet, 19% after the first interview, 35% after the second

support.sentence: In the second interview, the false memory rate further increased to 35% (33 partial memories, 10 full memories).
support.readBy: memory-rewritten reviser, 2026-11-26: PsyArXiv nh3zq, Results (15%, 19%, 35% in 3 sentences)

findings.text: Asked themselves at the end, 14% said they remembered the made-up event (against 35% coded by the researchers)

support.sentence: When asked whether they remembered the fake lost in the mall story, 14% of participants reported that they did (this compares to an interview 2 coded false memory rate of 35%).
support.readBy: memory-rewritten reviser, 2026-11-26: accepted version, PsyArXiv nh3zq, Results, self-report

findings.text: A further 52% did not remember the made-up event but believed it had happened

support.sentence: A further 52% reported that though they did not remember the fake event, they believed it had occurred.
support.readBy: memory-rewritten reviser, 2026-11-26: accepted version, PsyArXiv nh3zq, Results, self-report

limits: a reanalysis of the transcripts (andrews-2024-mall) finds few suggested details recalled and many reports that may be real memories; the authors replied in 2025
the coders' 35% and the participants' own 14% differ; the authors: the false memory rate « may be closer to 14% »
one country, 123 people; getting lost is a mild childhood fright, not a harmless everyday event
3 people may have had a true memory of being lost; without them, 33% (full text)
